title: Stony Brook Site
summary: The Stony Brook Site is an archaeological site in Stony Brook, New York, connected with Archaic-period Native occupation near the North Shore area of Aunt Amy's Creek. Excavations by William A. Ritchie and later archaeologists helped document long Indigenous presence, toolmaking, shellfish use, and the need to protect archaeological places from disturbance.
activity_update_summary: Consolidated the dated Stony Brook research into cited Historic Moments and moved its stewardship questions into a clearly formatted learning section.
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Setauket Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: Excavations along Aunt Amy's Creek at the Stony Brook Site have uncovered the physical remains of semi-permanent camps used by pre-ceramic Archaic groups thousands of years ago. Preserving the memory of these early habitation sites provides tangible evidence of the deep, enduring history of Indigenous peoples adapting to and thriving within Long Island's coastal ecosystems.
artifacts_content:
Excavators catalogued 101 projectile points among 131 non-pottery objects, along with eight bone implements, one small shell ornament, and pottery fragments. William A. Ritchie relied heavily on projectile-point typology when interpreting the age and relationships of the material, a common archaeological method at the time.

The Orient complex is an archaeological classification for certain Late Archaic and Transitional-period materials; it is not the name of an Indigenous nation or community. The stone tools, pottery, shell, animal remains, burned stone, and quartz document toolmaking, foodways, and daily life near Stony Brook without identifying the people through an archaeological label.

excavation_content:
William A. Ritchie's account of the 1955 excavation of the Stony Brook Site Unlike the majority of archaeological sites on Long Island and, indeed, throughout much of the Northeast, the Stony Brook site, although known to a few local people, was undisturbed when reported in July 1955 to William H. Sears of the reconnaissance party of the State Museum, by Mr. P. Roger Smith of Stony Brook, whose unselfish cooperation is gratefully acknowledged. Because of the site's intact condition it was possible from the start of operations to plan and execute a systematic excavation and to discern vital stratigraphic relations which are often largely obscured on a heavily vandalized site. When brought to [Ritchie's] attention, the tract of land containing the site had already been surveyed into residential building lots and comprised section 3 of the Stony Brook Shores Corporation, although construction had not yet begun. [Ritchie's] request for permission to explore the land, made through the corporation's vice president, Mr. T. Bayles Minuse, brought enthusiastic and generous support, for which our [The New York State Museum] hearty thanks are expressed to Mr. Minuse and other members of the corporation. The preliminary work of 1955, carried out by the writer, assisted by William R. Young and Walter F. Knowlson, consumed 16 days and consisted in the excavation of 12 5-foot sections of the site, from which I inferred its potential significance as a habitation site of the Orient complex. Between July 11 and August 19, 1956, an additional 55 squares were explored by a party comprising James V. Wright, Galen B. Ritchie and John W. Fenton II, under a research grant generously made to the Board of Regents by Mr. Ward Melville of Stony Brook. During the first week this party was reinforced by the State Museum unit comprising William R. Young, Douglas F. Jordan and the writer. Later, by alternating between the two parties, when the Museum unit conducted the Sugar Loaf Hill and Wading River digs, the writer actively directed the work of both groups. When, at the close of the 1956 field season at Stony Brook, it became evident that the greater part of the site had been thoroughly investigated, Mr. Melville further expressed his interest by making a second grant in aid for publishing the results of the researches and to procure radiocarbon analyses of charcoal samples from the site. On behalf of all concerned, it is a pleasure to record our grateful thanks to Mr. Melville. Features found on the site were neither numerous nor complex. For the most part they comprised pits, hearths and a single burial. [1. William A. Ritchie, The Stony Brook Site and It's Relation to Archaic and Transitional Cultures of Long Island, 1959 pp 13]
Originally excavated by William A. Ritchie in 1959, and again in 1969; the Stony Brook Site was studied by Ritchie & Funk in 1973, again by B. Salwen in 1962 and 1965, and most recently by Lynn Ceci in 1977.
vandalism_content: The written report of this site describes the contemporary landscape as an "Area possibly destroyed by housing development."
